newsitem.title: USA: HMO group seeks to clarify emergency policy.
newsitem.headline: HMO group seeks to clarify emergency policy.

text.p: The leading managed care umbrella group Thursday said it was urging member health plans to cover emergency room care if the patient's symptoms "reasonably appear" to constitute a real emergency.

The American Association of Health Plans has been urging its members to clarify its policies in a number of controversial areas, such as emergency coverage, where the industry has been criticised and where some lawmakers have proposed tighter regulation.

There have been numerous anecdotal reports of people going to the emergency room with a condition that turned out not to be a true emergency and then having trouble getting their health plan to cover the cost.
This could be chest pains that turn out to be indigestion, not a heart attack, or a stomach ache that turned out to be a run-of-the mill virus, not appendicitis.

The health group, which represents health maintenance organisations and other managed care groups, said: "Health plans should cover emergency-room screening and stabilisation as needed for conditions that reasonably appear to constitute an emergency, based on the patient's presenting symptoms.
"Emergency conditions are those that arise suddenly and require immediate treatment to avoid jeopardy to a patient's life or health," it said.
The patient's regular physician should be contacted as soon as possible, and the emergency room should not be used for what are clear non-emergencies, the group said.
In addition, the industry group said that health plans should make clear their reasons for denying coverage of treatment and explain patients' right to appeal.
An advocacy group that has been a sharp critic of the managed care industry, called the Patient Access to Speciality Care Coalition, dismissed the policy as "smoke and mirrors."

The coalition said it was an "example of how the industry is responding to increasing criticism of its policies with another empty gesture." The coalition supports greater federal regulation to ensure patients have a choice of doctors.
